title: Resting-state brain networks alterations in adolescents with Internet Gaming Disorder associate with cognitive control impairments.
response: This study (PMID: 39315326) investigated the neural mechanisms underlying cognitive control impairments in adolescents with Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD). The researchers found that impulsivity in adolescent IGD subjects was positively correlated with the severity of IGD, and was associated with alterations in the Executive Control Network (ECN) and the Salience Network (SN). Specifically, decreased functional connectivity between the SN and ECN, as well as decreased resting state activity of the dorsal attention network (DAN), were linked to attentional dysregulation and impulsivity in adolescents with IGD. Notably, the degree of IGD was positively correlated with enhanced functional connectivity between the ECN and DAN. These findings suggest that changes in the ECN and DAN may contribute to the development of impulsivity and attentional deficits in adolescents with IGD. The study's results provide new insights into the neurobiological mechanisms underlying cognitive control impairments in IGD, and highlight the importance of examining the relationship between cognitive control disorders and resting-state brain networks in this population.

title: Role of White Matter Microstructure in Impulsive Behavior.
response:
A recent study (PMID: 35040662) investigated the relationship between white matter microstructure and impulsivity in healthy individuals. The researchers used diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to examine the association between impulsivity and white matter fractional anisotropy (FA) values in 74 healthy adults. 

The results showed that whole-brain FA was inversely correlated with motor impulsiveness and positively correlated with nonplanning impulsiveness. Specifically, motor impulsiveness was associated with lower FA values in the corticospinal tract, while nonplanning impulsiveness was linked to higher FA values in the superior fronto-occipital fasciculus. These findings suggest that impulsivity is a network-based construct involving white matter microstructural integrity, and that specific white matter tracts may be involved in different aspects of impulsivity.

This study provides evidence that altered white matter microstructure may underlie normal individual variability in impulsive behaviors, and highlights the importance of considering the neural basis of impulsivity in both healthy and clinical populations. The findings have implications for the development of novel treatments targeting white matter microstructure to reduce impulsivity in individuals with neuropsychiatric illnesses.

title: The Relationship Between Impulsivity Traits and In Vivo Cerebral Serotonin Transporter and Serotonin 2A Receptor Binding in Healthy Individuals: A Double-Tracer PET Study with C-11 DASB and C-11 MDL100907.
response: A recent study (PMID: 39796107) investigated the relationship between impulsivity traits and serotonergic activity in healthy individuals using positron emission tomography (PET) with two tracers: [11C]DASB and [11C]MDL100907. The study found that non-planning impulsiveness was positively correlated with 5-HT2A receptor binding potential (BPND) in several brain regions, including the caudate, prefrontal cortex, and amygdala. These findings suggest that impulsivity traits may be associated with serotonergic neurotransmission, particularly 5-HT2A receptor-mediated postsynaptic signaling. The study's results also indicate that motor impulsiveness was positively correlated with serotonin transporter binding potential in the caudate. Overall, this study provides evidence that impulsivity is linked to altered serotonergic activity in key brain regions involved in executive function, judgment, and inhibitory control.

title: Electrophysiological Activity Prior to Self-initiated Movements is Related to Impulsive Personality Traits.
response: A recent neuroimaging study (PMID: 29337234) investigated the relationship between impulsivity and neural activity prior to self-initiated movements. The study found a positive correlation between impulsivity, as measured by the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11), and motor system excitability during movement preparation. Specifically, individuals with higher impulsivity scores showed an earlier negative rising phase and greater amplitude of the readiness potential (RP), a neural signal associated with motor preparation. These findings suggest that trait impulsivity may be characterized by less effective preparatory inhibition mechanisms, which could contribute to the control of behavior. This study provides evidence that impulsivity is related to differences in neural activity prior to movement onset, and highlights the potential role of neuroimaging in understanding the neural mechanisms underlying impulsive behavior.

title: Impulsivity, gender, and response to fenfluramine challenge in borderline personality disorder.
response:
A PubMed abstract (PMID: 12860356) suggests that impulsivity in borderline personality disorder (BPD) is linked to reduced central serotonergic function. A study of 64 BPD subjects (20 males, 44 females) and 57 controls found that male BPD subjects had lower prolactin responses to a fenfluramine challenge compared to male controls. 

The study also found that impulsivity and aggression predicted prolactin responses, and that when impulsivity was accounted for, the effect of BPD diagnosis on prolactin response was eliminated. Furthermore, impulsivity and aggression were inversely related to prolactin responses in male but not female subjects. 

These findings suggest that impulsivity may be a key factor in the relationship between BPD and central serotonergic function, and that gender differences in this relationship may exist. The study's results have implications for understanding the neurobiological basis of impulsivity in BPD and for developing targeted treatments for this population.

title: Enhanced ADHD classification through deep learning and dynamic resting state fMRI analysis.
response:
This study (PMID: 39424632) investigated the use of deep learning and dynamic resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) analysis to classify Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) from typically developing children (TDC). The researchers developed a novel deep learning-based network, Skip-Vote-Net, which leveraged dynamic connectivity analysis on rs-fMRI data to classify ADHD subtypes.

The study found that Skip-Vote-Net achieved high classification accuracies for ADHD, particularly in distinguishing between the inattentive subtype (ADHDI) and the predominantly combined subtype (ADHDC). The results suggest that dynamic changes in functional connectivity patterns among ADHD children can be effectively captured using Skip-Vote-Net, which may have potential as an effective diagnostic tool for identifying ADHD subtypes and distinguishing ADHD from TDC.

Notably, the study highlights the importance of impulsivity in ADHD, as it is a core symptom of the disorder. The use of rs-fMRI analysis and deep learning-based networks like Skip-Vote-Net may provide valuable insights into the neural mechanisms underlying impulsivity in ADHD, which could inform the development of more effective treatments.

title: Ventromedial prefrontal value signals and functional connectivity during decision-making in suicidal behavior and impulsivity.
response:
This study (PMID: 32035425) investigated the neural underpinnings of impulsivity and suicidal behavior using neuroimaging techniques. The researchers found that individuals with a history of suicide attempts showed reduced ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) value activation during decision-making tasks compared to nonpsychiatric controls. 

The study also explored the relationship between impulsivity and vmPFC-frontoparietal connectivity in nonpsychiatric controls and compared it among patient groups. The results showed that impulsivity negatively moderated vmPFC-frontoparietal connectivity in nonpsychiatric controls, but this effect was abolished in individuals with a history of suicide attempts. 

These findings suggest that disrupted vmPFC value signals and altered vmPFC-frontoparietal connectivity patterns may contribute to the development of suicidal behavior in individuals with impulsivity. The study's results highlight the importance of considering the neural mechanisms underlying impulsivity and suicidal behavior in the development of effective treatments. 

The study's findings also suggest that the relationship between impulsivity and vmPFC-frontoparietal connectivity is specific to the vmPFC and not the striatum, which may have implications for the development of targeted interventions for individuals with suicidal behavior and impulsivity.

title: Exploring variability in basal ganglia connectivity with functional MRI in healthy aging.
response:
A recent study (PMID: 29442271) investigated the relationship between functional connectivity within the basal ganglia network (BGN) and various factors in healthy older adults. The study found that age was the only consistent correlate of BGN functional connectivity, with older adults showing reduced connectivity. 

Interestingly, the study also explored the relationship between BGN functional connectivity and impulsivity, but found no significant association. This suggests that impulsivity may not be directly linked to changes in BGN functional connectivity in healthy aging. 

The study's findings are in line with previous research suggesting that changes in BGN functional connectivity are more closely related to age-related alterations in the dopaminergic system rather than other factors such as impulsivity. 

This study's results have implications for our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying healthy aging and the potential impact of age-related changes on brain function. However, further research is needed to fully understand the relationship between BGN functional connectivity and impulsivity in both healthy and diseased populations.

title: Head Motion and Inattention/Hyperactivity Share Common Genetic Influences: Implications for fMRI Studies of ADHD.
response:
This study (PMID: 26745144) investigated the relationship between head motion (HM) and impulsivity/hyperactivity in individuals with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). The researchers used neuroimaging data from resting-state functional MRI (fMRI) and maternal and self-report measures of impulsivity/hyperactivity from the Strengths and Weaknesses of ADHD Symptoms and Normal Behaviour (SWAN) scales. 

The study found that HM was moderately correlated with maternal reports of impulsivity/hyperactivity, suggesting a shared genetic influence. Specifically, the genetic correlations between HM and impulsivity/hyperactivity were 0.24 and 0.23, indicating that a significant portion of the association between HM and impulsivity/hyperactivity can be attributed to pleiotropic genetic factors. 

The study's findings have important implications for fMRI studies of ADHD, as treating HM as a nuisance covariate may reduce power to detect between-group effects and increase the likelihood of false positives. title: Converging Evidence for Frontopolar Cortex as a Target for Neuromodulation in Addiction Treatment.
response:
Evidence Summary: Impulsivity and Neuroimaging

Recent neuroimaging studies suggest that the frontopolar cortex may be a key region for targeting in addiction treatment. This area has been identified as a promising therapeutic target for transcranial brain stimulation in substance use disorders, supported by converging multimodal evidence from lesion-based maps, functional MRI-based maps, tES studies, TMS studies, and dose-response relationships (PMID: 38018143). 

The frontopolar cortex has been implicated in impulsivity, a common trait among individuals with substance use disorders. By targeting this region with transcranial brain stimulation, clinicians may be able to improve clinical outcomes in individuals with substance use disorders. The review highlights the importance of considering interindividual variations in brain state and trait, as well as electric field distribution patterns, when tailoring treatment. This approach may lead to improved treatment outcomes through optimization of treatment dimensions such as context, target, dose, and timing.

title: Individual Differences in Delay Discounting are Associated with Dorsal Prefrontal Cortex Connectivity in Youth.
response:
This study investigated the neural basis of impulsivity in youth, specifically examining the relationship between delay discounting and functional connectivity in the brain. 

The researchers found that individual differences in delay discounting, a measure of impulsive choice, were associated with patterns of connectivity emanating from the left dorsal prefrontal cortex (DPC), a key region of the default mode network. 

Notably, delay discounting was linked to increased connectivity between the DPC and other parts of the default mode network, as well as reduced connectivity with regions involved in attentional and cognitive control, such as the dorsal and ventral attention networks. 

These findings suggest that impulsivity in youth may be related to altered functional connectivity within and between key brain networks, including the default mode network and attentional networks. 

This study contributes to our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying impulsivity and may have implications for the development of targeted interventions to reduce impulsive behavior in youth. 

The study's use of resting-state fMRI and multivariate analysis techniques provides a comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the complex relationships between brain function and behavior.

title: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation-Induced Plasticity Improving Cognitive Control in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, Part II: Task-Based Neural Predictors of Treatment Response.
response:
This study (39284401) investigated the use of task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to predict clinical outcomes in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) patients undergoing repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with exposure with response prevention psychotherapy. 

The study found that pretreatment fMRI-derived measures of task-related brain activation and connectivity during planning and inhibitory control tasks were associated with clinical response to rTMS in OCD patients. Specifically, higher activation in task-relevant regions and lower error-related activation were correlated with better short-term clinical improvement in the vertex group. In contrast, lower precuneus activation with increased planning taskload was associated with symptom reduction in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex group, while higher error-related activation and lower inhibition-related insular-amygdalar connectivity were linked to symptom reduction in the presupplementary motor area group.

These findings suggest that neuroimaging measures of impulsivity and cognitive control, such as task-related brain activation and connectivity, may be useful in predicting treatment response to rTMS in OCD patients. However, the study's results also highlight the importance of considering individual differences in brain function and the need for larger sample sizes and placebo-controlled trials to further validate these findings.

title: Prefrontal Cortical Connectivity Mediates Locus Coeruleus Noradrenergic Regulation of Inhibitory Control in Older Adults.
response:
This study (35277392) investigated the relationship between impulsivity and neuroimaging in older adults. The researchers used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to examine the integrity of the locus coeruleus noradrenergic system, which is responsible for regulating inhibitory control. They found that better response inhibition was correlated with locus coeruleus integrity and stronger connectivity between the presupplementary motor area (preSMA) and right inferior frontal gyrus (rIFG). 

The study's results suggest that the locus coeruleus noradrenergic system plays a significant role in regulating inhibitory control, and that this effect is mediated by prefrontal cortical connectivity. The researchers also found that age moderated the relationship between locus coeruleus integrity and inhibitory control, indicating that the effect of the locus coeruleus on behavior changes with age.

These findings provide evidence that impulsivity is associated with differences in brain structure and function, specifically in the locus coeruleus and prefrontal cortex. The study's results have implications for the development of treatment strategies for impulsive clinical populations, and suggest that age and locus coeruleus integrity may be important factors to consider when designing these interventions.

title: Time scale properties of task and resting-state functional connectivity: Detrended partial cross-correlation analysis.
response:
This study (PMID: 29454934) investigated the time scale properties of functional connectivity in the brain during rest and task states using fMRI data from 68 subjects. The researchers employed a novel measure, detrended partial cross-correlation analysis (DPCCA), to examine correlations between brain regions at different time scales. 

The results showed that the time scales of within-network connectivity in the default mode network (DMN) and task networks were modulated in opposite directions across rest and task states. Specifically, the time scale increased during rest compared to task in the DMN, while it decreased in task networks.

Notably, the study found a significant correlation between the within-network connectivity time scale of the pre-supplementary motor area (a region critical for proactive inhibitory control) and impulsivity. The results showed that individuals with higher impulsivity (as measured by the Barratt impulsivity scale) had shorter within-network connectivity time scales in this region, which was also associated with longer stop signal reaction times. 

These findings suggest that the time scale properties of brain networks may vary across mental states and provide evidence for the role of low-frequency fluctuations of BOLD signals in behavioral control, particularly in relation to impulsivity.

title: Identifying a Biological Signature of Trauma-Related Neurodegeneration Following Repeated Traumatic Brain Injuries Compared with Healthy Controls.
response:
This study investigated the relationship between repeated traumatic brain injuries (TBIs) and neurodegeneration, comparing participants with a history of TBIs to healthy controls. The study found that despite a higher symptom burden, participants with TBIs did not exhibit significant differences in core diagnostic biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease (AD) compared to controls. However, volumetrics in critical brain regions, particularly the amygdala, were associated with several symptom domains in the TBI group.

Notably, the study found that impulsivity, as measured by the Barratt Impulsivity Scale (BIS), was associated with amygdala normative percentile and/or amygdala asymmetry index in the TBI group. This suggests that impulsivity may be linked to changes in the amygdala, a region critical for emotional processing and regulation.

The study's findings have implications for the development of early biomarkers for chronic symptom burden in individuals with a history of TBIs. While PET scans may not be sensitive enough to detect neuropathology in this population, volumetrics in critical brain regions, such as the amygdala, may provide a more viable early indicator of chronic symptom burden.

title: Response inhibition and impulsivity: an fMRI study.
response:

The study found that response inhibition was most prominent in the right lateral orbitofrontal cortex, with additional activation in the superior temporal gyrus, medial orbitofrontal cortex, cingulate gyrus, and inferior parietal lobule, predominantly on the right side.

The study also explored the relationship between impulsivity and neural response during response inhibition. Results showed that subjects with greater impulsivity scores and those who made more errors had greater activation of paralimbic areas, while less impulsive individuals and those with fewer errors activated higher order association areas. Notably, the study found a strong association between posterior orbital activation and Eysenck's impulsivity score, suggesting that greater engagement of the right orbitofrontal cortex is needed to maintain behavioral inhibition in impulsive individuals.

Interestingly, the study found that lower IQ was a more significant predictor of errors of commission during the task than impulsivity scores. title: Add-on repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in patients with opioid use disorder undergoing methadone maintenance therapy.
response:

The results suggest that rTMS may have a beneficial effect on impulsivity, as measured by the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale-11 (BIS-11), particularly in the attentional subscale. The active rTMS group showed significant improvements in BIS-11 attentional subscales compared to the sham group (P = 0.04). Additionally, the active rTMS group had lower commission T-scores (C-TS) on the Continuous Performance Tests (CPTs), indicating improved attention (P = 0.02). These findings suggest that rTMS may be a useful adjunctive treatment for reducing impulsivity and improving attention in individuals with OUD.

title: Functional connectivity in resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) in opioid use disorder.
response:
This evidence summary focuses on the relationship between impulsivity and neuroimaging, specifically resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), in individuals with opioid use disorder.

Research has shown that individuals with opioid addiction exhibit significant disruptions in functional connectivity within key brain networks, including the default mode network (DMN) and salience network (SN) (PMID: 41098388). These networks are involved in cognitive functions such as decision-making and impulse control. The DMN is responsible for introspection and self-reflection, while the SN is involved in detecting and responding to salient stimuli.

The study found that individuals with opioid addiction had altered functional connectivity within these networks, which may contribute to impulsivity and other cognitive deficits. The DMN and SN are critical for regulating impulse control, and disruptions in these networks may lead to impulsive behaviors.

The use of rs-fMRI has provided valuable insights into the neural mechanisms underlying opioid addiction and impulsivity. This non-invasive imaging technique allows researchers to examine functional connectivity in the brain while participants are at rest, providing a unique window into the neural networks involved in addiction and impulsivity.

title: Brain functional connectivity changes in children that differ in impulsivity temperamental trait.
response:
This study (PMID: 24834038) investigated the relationship between impulsivity and brain functional connectivity in typically developing children. The researchers used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure brain activity at rest and related it to impulsivity scores obtained from parents' questionnaires. 

Key findings include two default mode network (DMN) clusters, located at the posterior cingulate cortex and the right angular gyrus, which showed a negative correlation with impulsivity scores. The study also found that the impulsivity trait modulated the pattern of functional connectivity between the DMN and other brain networks, particularly reducing the anti-phasic relation between the DMN and action-related networks in high impulsive children.

These results suggest that impulsivity, as a personality trait, has a modulatory influence on the functional connectivity of resting-state brain networks in children. This study bridges the gap between developmental approaches and behavioral neuroscience by linking questionnaire-based data with brain structure and function. The findings provide evidence that impulsivity is associated with altered brain connectivity patterns, which may contribute to the development of behavioral problems in children.

title: Dissociable frontostriatal white matter connectivity underlies reward and motor impulsivity.
response:
A recent neuroimaging study (28189592) investigated the relationship between frontostriatal white matter connectivity and impulsivity in healthy individuals. The study used diffusion imaging data and probabilistic tractography to examine the association between white matter tracts and reward and motor impulsivity measures.

Key findings suggest that individual differences in white matter connectivity between the ventral striatum and prefrontal cortex regions (ventromedial and dorsolateral) are associated with reward impulsivity, as measured by delay discounting. In contrast, connectivity between the dorsal striatum and supplementary motor area is linked to motor impulsivity.

These results indicate that different types of impulsivity may be driven by distinct frontostriatal neural circuitry, supporting the idea of dissociable neural mechanisms underlying various forms of impulsive behavior. The study's findings also highlight the importance of structural connectivity in explaining behavioral variation, suggesting that white matter tracts play a critical role in modulating impulsive tendencies.

title: Dorsal striatal functional connectivity changes in Internet gaming disorder: A longitudinal magnetic resonance imaging study.
response:
This longitudinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study investigated the neural correlates of internet gaming disorder (IGD) in young males. The study found that individuals with IGD exhibited altered functional connectivity (FC) in the dorsal striatum, a brain region involved in reward processing and impulse control. Specifically, they showed decreased FC between the left dorsal putamen and left medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), suggesting a weakening of prefrontal control. In contrast, they exhibited increased FC between the right dorsal putamen and right middle occipital gyrus (MOG), indicating strengthening of the sensorimotor network.

These findings suggest that IGD may be associated with changes in the neural circuits underlying impulsivity and reward processing. The study's results also showed a significant correlation between changes in dorsal putamen-MOG FC and gaming time per day, indicating that the neural changes observed may be related to the severity of IGD.

The study's use of longitudinal MRI assessments allowed for the examination of changes in brain structure and function over time, providing valuable insights into the neural mechanisms underlying IGD. The findings have implications for the development of novel treatments for IGD, which may target the altered neural circuits involved in impulsivity and reward processing.

title: Delay discounting is associated with the fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations and resting-state functional connectivity in late adolescence.
response:
This study investigated the neural correlates of delay discounting (DD) in late adolescence using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (RS-fMRI). The results showed that higher DD was associated with increased fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF) in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), a region involved in conflict monitoring and strategy adaptation. Additionally, DD was positively correlated with resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) between the dACC and the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), a critical functional circuit in the cognitive control network.

These findings suggest that impulsivity, as measured by DD, is linked to altered neural activity and connectivity in regions involved in executive function and self-regulation. The study's results provide new insights into the neural basis of DD in adolescents and highlight the importance of considering individual differences in impulsivity when examining the neural correlates of decision-making.

The study's findings have implications for our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying impulsivity and decision-making in adolescents. title: Brain Networks Associated With COVID-19 Risk: Data From 3662 Participants.
response:
This study (PMID: 34993375) investigated the association between brain networks and COVID-19 risk in a large cohort of 3662 participants from the UK Biobank Resource. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans, the researchers identified six brain network fingerprints associated with COVID-19 positive status. The findings suggest that individuals with reduced connectivity in top-down attention and executive networks, such as the central executive and ventral salience networks, are at increased risk of COVID-19 infections. Conversely, increased internal connectivity within introspective and instinctive networks, such as the default mode, ventral salience, subcortical, and sensorimotor networks, was also linked to higher infection rates.

Notably, the study's results imply a potential link between brain network organization and impulsivity. The identified risk networks, characterized by reduced top-down control and increased internal connectivity, may be relevant to impulsivity and impulse control deficits. This is because top-down attention and executive networks are typically involved in regulating impulsive behaviors, whereas introspective and instinctive networks are often associated with automatic and impulsive processing. Therefore, the study's findings may have implications for the treatment of illnesses characterized by impulsivity, such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

title: Abnormal frontostriatal connectivity and serotonin function in gambling disorder: A preliminary exploratory study.
response:
A recent study (PMID: 37561637) investigated the neurobiological mechanisms underlying gambling disorder, focusing on frontostriatal connectivity and neurotransmitter systems. The study found that individuals with gambling disorder exhibited abnormal frontostriatal connectivity, specifically a loss of functional connectivity between the right nucleus accumbens (NAcc) and the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). 

Notably, the study also found that serotonergic function, as measured by 11C-MADAM binding, was significantly altered in individuals with gambling disorder. Specifically, right NAcc 11C-MADAM binding potential correlated with attentional impulsivity in individuals with gambling disorder, suggesting a link between serotonergic function and impulsivity in this population.

These findings contribute to our understanding of the neurobiological mechanisms underlying gambling disorder and may have implications for the development of treatments targeting this condition. The study's results highlight the importance of frontostriatal connectivity and serotonergic function in the pathophysiology of gambling disorder, and suggest that impulsivity may be a key symptom that is closely tied to these neural mechanisms.

title: Alterations in regional homogeneity of resting-state brain activity in internet gaming addicts.
response:
This study (PMID: 22901705) investigated the brain functions of internet gaming addicts (IGA) using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). The results showed that IGA subjects had altered regional homogeneity (ReHo) in various brain regions compared to healthy controls. Specifically, IGA subjects exhibited increased ReHo in brain regions associated with sensory-motor coordination, such as the brainstem, inferior parietal lobule, left posterior cerebellum, and left middle frontal gyrus. Conversely, they showed decreased ReHo in regions related to visual and auditory functions, including the temporal, occipital, and parietal lobes.

These findings suggest that long-term online gaming may lead to changes in brain activity patterns, particularly in regions involved in sensory-motor processing and regulation. The increased ReHo in sensory-motor coordination regions may indicate enhanced brain synchronization, potentially contributing to the addictive behavior. In contrast, the decreased ReHo in visual and auditory regions may reflect reduced excitability or decreased sensitivity to external stimuli, which could also contribute to the development of IGA.

Overall, this study provides evidence that impulsivity and neuroimaging are linked, as the altered brain activity patterns in IGA subjects may be related to the impulsive behavior associated with internet gaming

title: Associations between structural injury and task-based corticomuscular connectivity after stroke.
response:
This study investigated the relationship between structural injury and task-based corticomuscular connectivity after stroke (PMID: 41281564). The researchers used electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG) recordings during a grip task to assess corticomuscular coherence (CMC) in individuals with early subacute stroke. 

The study found that in individuals with mild-moderate corticospinal tract (CST) injury, greater injury was associated with higher CMC between specific cortical regions and muscles. Conversely, in individuals with higher CST integrity, CST integrity was positively related to CMC between other cortical regions and muscles. These findings suggest that post-stroke structural injury modulates task-based corticomuscular connectivity and highlight the complexity of structure-function relationships in stroke.

The study's results have implications for understanding the neural mechanisms underlying post-stroke recovery and may inform targeted rehabilitation strategies to optimize recovery. The findings also underscore the importance of considering individual differences in CST injury and integrity when investigating structure-function relationships in stroke.

title: Insula Connectivity Abnormalities Predict Impulsivity in Chronic Heroin Use Disorder: A Cross-Sectional Resting-State fMRI Study.
response:
A recent study (PMID: 38002468) investigated the neural correlates of impulsivity in individuals with chronic heroin use disorder (HUD) using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI). The study found that patients with HUD exhibited higher levels of trait impulsivity, particularly motor and nonplanning impulsivity, compared to healthy controls. 

The researchers used the insula as a seed point to examine the functional connectivity (FC) between the insula and the whole brain. They discovered that changes in FC between the right insula and certain brain regions, including the lateral occipital cortex and the right angular gyrus, were positively correlated with total trait impulsivity scores and specific impulsivity subtypes. Conversely, changes in FC between the left insula and the left superior frontal gyrus and left frontopolar brain region were negatively correlated with trait impulsivity.

These findings suggest that the insula may play a critical role in impulsivity and could serve as a potential biomarker for identifying trait impulsivity in patients with HUD. The study's results contribute to our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying impulsivity in addiction and highlight the importance of examining the intrinsic factor structure of impulsivity in HUD.

title: Negative correlation between right prefrontal activity during response inhibition and impulsiveness: a fMRI study.
response: A study published in 2004 (PMID: 15309395) investigated the relationship between impulsivity and brain activity during a Go/No-Go task using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). The study found that individuals with higher motor impulsiveness showed reduced activity in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (RDLPFC) during response inhibition. This suggests that the RDLPFC may play a key role in regulating impulsivity, with reduced activity in this region potentially contributing to impulsive behavior. The findings support the idea that neuroimaging can be used to identify individual differences in impulsivity and may have implications for understanding the neural mechanisms underlying impulsive behavior.

title: Impulsivity is related to overhasty risk learning in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A computational psychiatric approach.
response:

The researchers used a computational modeling approach and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data to examine how impulsivity influences the cognitive process of risk learning.

title: Go/No-Go task performance predicts differences in compulsivity but not in impulsivity personality traits.
response: A recent study (28783574) investigated the relationship between performance on the Go/No-Go task, a measure of response inhibition, and personality traits related to impulsivity and compulsivity. The study found that individuals who performed poorly on the task, as indicated by high false alarms, exhibited higher levels of compulsivity, as measured by the Maudsley Obsessional Compulsive Questionnaire (MOCI). title: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging alterations in borderline personality disorder: A systematic review.
response:

The review highlights the need for future studies to explore the neural correlates of BPD using multimodal methodologies and longitudinal designs. This could provide a better understanding of the complex relationships between brain function, impulsivity, and other symptoms of BPD.

title: A multimodal study of impulsivity and body weight: Integrating behavioral, cognitive, and neuroimaging approaches.
response:
A recent study (PMID: 27896939) investigated the relationship between impulsivity and body weight using a multimodal approach, incorporating behavioral, cognitive, and neuroimaging techniques. The study found positive correlations between body mass index (BMI) and both trait and state impulsivity, suggesting that individuals with higher BMI tend to exhibit more impulsive behaviors.

Neuroimaging results revealed that individuals with higher BMI showed reduced activation in the temporal lobe and insula during successful response inhibition, indicating impaired inhibitory control. Additionally, there was a positive association between BMI and functional connectivity between the right inferior frontal gyrus and right middle frontal gyrus during successful response inhibition.

Mediation analysis revealed that trait impulsivity, as measured by the impulsive sensation-seeking scale (ImpSS), mediated the relationship between BMI and neural response in the right inferior frontal gyrus. This suggests that trait impulsivity may play a key role in the neural mechanisms underlying the relationship between impulsivity and body weight.

Overall, this study provides evidence that impulsivity is a critical factor in the development and maintenance of obesity, and highlights the need to address inhibitory control mechanisms in weight management programs.

title: Altered functional connectivity in default mode network in Internet gaming disorder: Influence of childhood ADHD.
response:
This evidence summary focuses on the relationship between impulsivity and neuroimaging findings in individuals with internet gaming disorder (IGD).

Research has shown that individuals with IGD exhibit altered functional connectivity in the default mode network (DMN), particularly in regions associated with executive control and salience processing (28174127). Specifically, IGD subjects without childhood ADHD demonstrated expanded functional connectivity between DMN-related regions and brain areas involved in salience processing, whereas those with childhood ADHD showed increased connectivity between the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and the cerebellum, a region implicated in executive control.

Notably, the strength of connectivity between the PCC and cerebellum was positively correlated with self-reported impulsiveness in IGD subjects with childhood ADHD. This suggests that altered neural networks for executive control in ADHD may predispose individuals to developing IGD, and that impulsivity may be a key factor in this relationship.

These findings highlight the importance of considering the interplay between childhood ADHD and IGD in understanding the neural mechanisms underlying impulsivity and executive control deficits in IGD. Further research is needed to elucidate the complex relationships between these factors and to inform the development of effective interventions for IGD.

title: Impaired corticostriatal connectivity in impulse control disorders in Parkinson disease.
response:

The researchers used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine resting-state corticostriatal connectivity in 20 PD patients with ICDs, 19 PD patients without ICDs, and 19 healthy controls.

The study found that PD patients with ICDs exhibited impaired connectivity between the left anterior putamen and key brain regions, including the left inferior temporal gyrus and the left anterior cingulate gyrus. In contrast, PD patients without ICDs and healthy controls showed normal corticostriatal connectivity. These findings suggest that ICDs in PD are associated with disrupted neural communication between the striatum and cortical regions involved in impulse control.

The study's results have implications for understanding the neural basis of impulsivity in PD and may inform the development of targeted treatments for ICDs in this population.

title: Human Brain Imaging Links Dopaminergic Systems to Impulsivity.
response:

Key findings suggest that striatal D2-type dopamine receptors (D2 and D3) and corticostriatal connectivity play a crucial role in cognitive control. Low levels of striatal and midbrain D2-type receptor availability were found to correlate with self-reported impulsivity, while striatal D2-type receptor availability showed a positive correlation with motor response inhibition and cognitive flexibility.

Furthermore, the study found an inverted U-shaped function between striatal D2-type dopamine receptor availability and impulsive choice on reward-based decision-making tasks, indicating an optimal level of striatal dopaminergic activity. These findings have significant implications for the development of therapeutic targets to improve cognitive control, particularly in clinical populations with striatal dopamine D2-type receptor deficits.

Overall, this research highlights the importance of striatal dopaminergic systems in impulsivity and provides a foundation for further investigation into the neural mechanisms underlying this complex behavior.

title: Emotion dysregulation, impulsivity and anger rumination in borderline personality disorder: the role of amygdala and insula.

The study also found reduced functional connectivity between the amygdala and other brain regions, including the frontal pole, precuneus, and temporal pole, in BPD patients. This reduced connectivity correlated with anger rumination and impulsivity. title: The Effect of Mindfulness Meditation on Impulsivity and its Neurobiological Correlates in Healthy Adults.
response:
A recent study published in Scientific Reports (PMID: 31427669) investigated the effect of mindfulness meditation on impulsivity and its neurobiological correlates in healthy adults. The study found that an eight-week mindfulness intervention did not significantly reduce impulsivity in participants, as measured by the go/no-go task and the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11). 

Interestingly, long-term meditators (LTMs) reported lower attentional impulsivity but higher motor and non-planning impulsivity on the BIS-11 compared to meditation-naïve participants (MNPs). Neuroimaging results showed that LTMs had less striatal gray matter, greater cortico-striatal-thalamic functional connectivity, and lower spontaneous eye-blink rate (a physiological dopamine indicator) than MNPs. 

However, the study's findings suggest that neither short-term nor long-term mindfulness practice may be effective in reducing impulsive behavior in healthy adults, particularly those with inhibitory motor control or planning capacity deficits. The lack of significant relationships between total lifetime practice hours (TLPH) and impulsivity or neurobiological metrics further supports this conclusion, suggesting that pre-existing differences between LTMs and MNPs may be responsible for the observed differences.

The results showed that high-impulsive individuals exhibited a greater reliance on model-free control, which is associated with habitual behavior, and reduced model-based signatures in the right lateral prefrontal cortex. This suggests that individuals with high impulsivity may be more prone to habitual behavior and less able to engage in goal-directed control. 

Interestingly, the study found that gray matter density in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex was positively associated with model-based control, regardless of impulsivity levels. This implies that individual differences in brain structure may influence the ability to engage in goal-directed behavior. 

Overall, the study provides evidence that impulsivity is associated with altered neural control mechanisms, specifically a greater reliance on model-free control and reduced model-based control in the right lateral prefrontal cortex. These findings have implications for our understanding of the neural basis of impulsivity and may inform the development of interventions to reduce impulsivity and promote goal-directed behavior.

title: Neural Basis of Increased Cognitive Control of Impulsivity During the Mid-Luteal Phase Relative to the Late Follicular Phase of the Menstrual Cycle.
response:
This evidence summary focuses on the relationship between impulsivity, neuroimaging, and the menstrual cycle.

Research has shown that hormonal fluctuations across the menstrual cycle influence reward-related motivation and impulsive behaviors (PMID: 33304251). A study published in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2020 found that women in the late follicular phase (FP) were more impulsive than those in the mid-luteal phase (LP), as evidenced by their greater responsiveness to short-term rewards and increased activity in the dorsal striatum (DS). 

The study also found that the dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) played a crucial role in regulating impulsivity, with functional connectivity between the DS and dlPFC correlating with discount rate and psychometric impulsivity scores. Notably, the right dlPFC was more active in the mid-LP than in the late FP, and this effect was sensitive to estradiol levels.

These findings suggest that cyclical gonadal hormones affect cognitive control of impulsive behavior in a periodic manner, possibly via DS-dlPFC circuitry. The study's results have implications for the treatment of conditions characterized by hyper-impulsivity, such as obsessive-compulsive disorder, Parkinson's disease, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

title: Nature of functional links in valuation networks differentiates impulsive behaviors between abstinent heroin-dependent subjects and nondrug-using subjects.
response: This 2015 NeuroImage study (PMID: 25944613) investigated the neural correlates of impulsivity in abstinent heroin-dependent individuals and nondrug-using controls using resting-state functional MRI. The study found that the functional link between the reward system (β-network) and the executive control system (δ-network) influences impulsivity. In nondrug-using controls, the link between these networks is balanced, with the executive control system competitively controlling impulsivity. However, in abstinent heroin-dependent individuals, the link is imbalanced, with stronger connectivity between the reward system and weaker connectivity between the executive control system and the reward system. This imbalance is associated with impulsivity, suggesting that the reward and executive control systems may mutually reinforce each other in individuals with a history of heroin dependence. These findings may provide insight into the neural mechanisms underlying drug addiction and impulsivity, and may serve as a potential endophenotype for identifying individual differences in self-control capacity.

title: Investigation of structure-function correlation among the young offspring of patients with bipolar disorder.

Specifically, higher MD values in the cingulum were associated with higher impulsivity scores. The study's results provide evidence that impulsivity is associated with specific neuroimaging findings in a high-risk group for bipolar disorder. These findings suggest that different cognitive control subsystems are involved in impulsivity, and that impulsivity trait components may be attributed to distinct neural mechanisms. 

This study provides evidence that impulsivity is a complex trait with multiple underlying neural mechanisms, and that different components of impulsivity may be associated with distinct cognitive control processes.
